### Why the version jumps from 0.1.11 to 0.2.0

From this release the second number means "**you have to do something after upgrading, or a host
on the older version loses a capability**". The third is everything else. This release is the
latter: following a host to a new address now requires it to establish who it is, which an older
version cannot do (see "A change in behaviour between versions" below).

Upgrading from 0.1.11 **does not require pairing again**.

### Security fixes

This release is about the local network attack surface. **All of these require a hostile machine
on the same network segment**, so the risk at home is low; but two of them need no knowledge of
your pairing password.

- **A stranger can no longer take over a paired host's address.** A host id is derived from a MAC
  address or hostname, with no secret in it, and is broadcast in the clear. Previously, anything
  advertising the same id and answering a Ping with any well-formed reply could get this computer
  to repoint the pairing at it permanently — after which every notice went there. A reply must now
  be signed with the pairing password before it is followed.
- **A silent connection can no longer exhaust the agent.** Connections were bounded in size but
  not in time, and nothing is authenticated until a whole request has arrived. Anyone able to
  reach the port could open connections, send nothing, and use up the resources that answer the
  paired computer's switch requests. There is now a deadline.
- **The pairing password is no longer readable by other accounts on the same computer.** It is
  stored in the settings file in the clear, and that file was written with no permissions set. It
  is now owner-only (on Windows the AppData ACL already denied it to other accounts).
- **Replies are size-bounded** the way requests already were.
- **The replay cache now expires by time.** It used to empty itself completely on reaching two
  thousand entries, which let every nonce it held be used once more.
- **The exact version is no longer broadcast**, which told everyone on the network precisely which
  known weaknesses a host has.
- **rustls updated to 0.23.45** (RUSTSEC-2026-0285), the TLS stack the update check uses.

### Fixed: a display's input resetting itself to "not selected"

The scan emptied a display's stored input and input list **before** going to read them, and that
read is allowed to fail — a display answers the host it is showing and no other, so failing is
the ordinary case for the host that is off screen. On failure the values were already gone, and
the caller logged it and saved the settings anyway.

The value came back on whichever later scan managed to read, which is why it looked like an input
disappearing and returning for no reason. **An input set by hand was discarded the same way** —
and setting it by hand exists precisely because this read cannot reach a computer the display has
never shown.

Nothing stored is discarded now. A reading replaces it; the absence of one does not.

### Fixed: display merges never actually applied between two hosts

**Windows reads this MSI's serial number and macOS reads none from it.** Merges were matched on a
full fingerprint comparison, which counts "one side has a serial, the other does not" as a
difference.

So a merge made on one computer arrived on the other, was stored, and matched nothing there. That
computer went on offering the same display for merging, and merging it again stored a second
entry — and since a merge card is labelled by manufacturer and product code only, the two were
identical on screen: one display merged into one display, listed twice.

**The change reaches only as far as a missing serial:**

- Two serials that are both present and different still mean two displays
- A serial present on one side only is treated as the same display
- **Switching is untouched** — a write still demands an exact fingerprint match against a display
  present right now, and refuses when more than one matches

Duplicate merges already stored are **collapsed to the newest when settings load**, so the
duplicate on screen goes away without unmerging anything.

### ⚠️ A change in behaviour between versions

**An address change is followed automatically only when both computers are on this version.**

An older host does not sign its replies and so cannot establish who it is, and this computer will
no longer follow it to a new address. If you update only one machine and the other's IP changes
via DHCP, **the pairing will not repair itself** — set the address by hand on the settings page,
or update both.

This is a deliberate trade: something that cannot establish who it is should not be trusted
automatically.

### Known limitations

- The **contents** of a reply are still unauthenticated. The signature establishes who answered
  and which request they answered; forged host order or input notes inside a reply could still be
  merged. Authenticating the payload needs a protocol version of its own and is the next step.
- The pairing password is used directly as the HMAC key with no KDF, and the minimum is still
  eight characters. Changing either would stop old and new versions communicating at all, so it
  needs a migration plan.
- Undoing a merge leaves the inputs and notes that merging folded into the display the other
  identity joined.
- Ports, input lists, host names, input notes and merges only sync between hosts running this
  version.
- The macOS DMG is ad-hoc signed but not notarized with an Apple Developer ID, so Gatekeeper may
  require manual approval.
